analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card fees for paying on time and requires notice before rate hikes.
analysis.headline: The Credit Card Consumer Protection Act of 1997 never got a vote: it sat in a House Banking subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to stop several credit card practices that add costs for cardholders: charging fees to customers who pay their balance in full on time, raising interest rates without advance notice or the chance to cancel and pay off the old balance, charging over-the-limit fees on transactions the card company itself approved, two-cycle billing (charging interest twice on a balance already partially paid), and low 'teaser' rates that hide the much higher permanent rate. It also required clear disclosure of fees on convenience checks. It was introduced by Rep. Joseph Kennedy II with 16 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, sent to its consumer credit subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit cardholders, especially people who carry a balance or occasionally pay late: they would keep the interest rate they signed up for unless notified 15 days ahead with a right to cancel and pay off at the old rate, and they would stop paying fees for paying on time, for going over their limit on the card company's own approved transactions, and for interest charged through two-cycle billing.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits minimum finance charges or fees imposed solely because a cardholder repaid the balance in full before the grace period ended [S2][S3].
Requires at least 15 days' advance notice of any interest rate increase, with notice of the right to cancel the card and pay the existing balance under the old rate and terms [S2][S3].
Prohibits over-the-limit fees on transactions the creditor approved in advance or at the time of the transaction [S2][S3].
Bans two-cycle billing, under which interest is charged on a balance already partially paid off during the grace period [S2][S3].
Requires applications and solicitations with short-term introductory rates to prominently disclose the permanent fixed or variable rate that applies afterward [S2][S3].
Requires disclosure of transaction fees and interest rates on credit advances made through third-party convenience checks [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose revenue from on-time-payment fees, retroactive rate increases on balances, over-limit fees on approved transactions, two-cycle interest, and customers drawn in by teaser rates they would now see priced honestly.

drawbacks.text: Some of the costs would likely be passed to cardholders through higher annual fees or interest rates on cards generally, since issuers would no longer recover them through the targeted fees [S3].

Requiring a 15-day notice-and-cancellation option for any rate increase would limit issuers' ability to reprice risk on existing balances, which could make credit harder to get or more expensive for borrowers with weaker credit histories [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections address practices widely seen as hidden or retroactive charges, and honest disclosure of teaser rates is a light-touch remedy. The tradeoff is that issuers would likely recover some costs through other fees or rates, and stricter repricing rules could modestly raise the price of credit for riskier borrowers. On balance the bill transfers costs from cardholders' surprise fees to more visible pricing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee and then to its consumer credit subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II introduced the bill on June 19, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].

On July 14, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it remained with no hearings, markup, or floor action through the end of the 105th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 16 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept the fee and rate practices the bill would have banned, including fees for on-time payments, retroactive rate increases, and two-cycle billing.

for.name: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Consumer Protection Act of 1997.

for.name: 16 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by a Republican in the 105th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled, and the bill died in its subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors were Democrats and there is no record of Republican support or committee action during the 105th Congress.

industries.note: The bill would have banned revenue practices that charge cardholders extra for paying on time, for approved over-limit transactions, and for two-cycle interest, and would have required advance notice before rate hikes. Issuers' gain from keeping those practices is paid for by cardholders' fees and interest [S2][S3].
